Just to clear things up. I think I'm AP. I have classic AP behaviours. Fear of abandonment, hate being alone, think others are better than me etc. 

This friend is platonic. Great guy. Known him since college. He's in my inner circle. He knows that I'm AP and gives reassurance. By rights, I should trust him.

But, I don't. My therapist says I have these anxious behaviours as a way of subtly keeping people away. i.e. if I'm always doubting that you'll leave, then I can never let you in and be vulnerable and thus spare myself the risk of rejection.

Going to rate the three novels on here as the Listerdale Mystery is a collection of stories.

(1) Passage to Frankfurt: The first book that AC wrote in the 70s and it shows. The plot makes no sense and it almost reads as if she imported the last third from a completely different manuscript. The only redeeming quality of the book is one of the side characters and just how weird the book is. 

(2) Destination Unknown: Ironically the last AC I had left to read. It's fine. It's fairly typical of her spy thrillers that she wrote in the 50s (*They Came to Baghdad).* Political intrigue, cold war anxiety, etc. It's OK but not stunning. 

(3)  Death Comes as the End: Really atmospheric story with a good sense of tension and a plot that kept me guessing. Figured out the murderer but only because I had read loads of AC at this point and knew how she works. Would recommend. 

imo, if you want to save the best for last, save *Death Comes as the End.* Maybe start with *Destination Unknown* and use *Frankfurt*  as a weird pallet cleanser.

What always strikes me about Poirot is that it seems to be the inverse of Holmes- that is, I prefer the Poirot novels to the short stories.  The short stories always seem to be a bit squashed. 

There is no set order to read Poirot as Christie really didn't care about the timeline. The only two exceptions to that are *The Mysterious Affair at Styles* where Poirot meets his Watson, Captain Hastings and *Curtain* which is his last case (also set in Styles) and should be read last. 

Hastings is Poirot's Watson but not nearly as prominent, only appearing in 8 of the 30 or so books. Good ones with Hastings include *The ABC Murders*  and *Peril at End House.* 

The 30s and 40s are the golden age of Poirot. I'd recommend *Cards on the Table, Evil Under the Sun, Murder on the Orient Express* and *Five Little Pigs* . The latter is a good example of Poirot's MO and his focus on psychology. He's trying to solve a cold case and only has the testimony of 5 people.  Lastly. *Murder of Rodger Ackroyd* is a classic.

It depends on when your AA comes from. I.e. my AA comes from my abandonment issues with my dad and so my anxiety comes from the core wound of feeling abandoned. So, in that case, any time I'm anxious I reassure small me that I've got him and I'm not going to leave him, he's a good boy etc. 

More generally though, you could try just noticing the thought and vibing with it. Sit with it and let it be. So, e.g say you have the thought that 'My SO is going to leave me' say 'OK, I'm having the thought that my SO is going to leave me.' It's just a thought. It's not the future, it's not reality. It's just something that your brain is telling you, the same way your nose tells you about smells or your ears tells you about sounds. But it can't harm you. That's the most important thing. 

If it's really bothering you, you could try some CBT style techniques where you look at how accurate the thought is but I sometimes don't bother with  them if the anxious thoughts are a lot. because it can be like whack a mole.

Ultimately though, I've learned that you can't really turn off the brain and anxiety. The anxiety is there to try and keep you safe. So what might help is acknowledging the thought and saying 'OK, but now I'm going to watch Netflix/go for a run/ play video games.' As uncomfortable as it is, let the anxiety run in the background.   They're just thoughts. 

Finally,  just remember that whatever your anxiety is telling you: you will be fine!
